U.S. Postal Service postmark practices that were formalized in a December 2025 rule could mean a longer delay between when something is mailed and when it's postmarked — a distinction that matters for tax returns, mail-in ballots and other time-sensitive documents.

The issue may crop up as two deadlines approach: Oct. 15 for taxpayers who received a six-month extension to file their federal income tax returns, and Nov. 3 for voters casting ballots in the midterm elections.

Taxpayers who mail their return can meet Thursday's deadline by taking it to the post office for a manual postmark. But voters casting ballots by mail for the midterms can't necessarily count on the same rule.

That's because while the IRS generally considers a return filed on the day it is postmarked, most states require mail-in ballots to arrive by Election Day, regardless of when they were mailed or postmarked. A postmark shows the date your mail was processed, which may not be the day you mailed the ballot.

Thirty-five states require mailed absentee ballots to be received by election officials on or before Election Day, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, a bipartisan organization that tracks state laws and policies. The other 15 states — along with Washington, Guam, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands — generally allow ballots postmarked by Election Day to arrive afterward, usually within a specified number of days.

"State laws govern elections for the most part, and every state has chosen a little bit different way of doing things," said Katy Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting for the NCSL.

## About 1.2% of 2024 mail-in ballots rejected

Nearly 48 million voters cast absentee ballots in the 2024 presidential election, representing roughly 30% of the total 158.2 million ballots cast, according to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission. The absentee figure includes mail-in ballots as well as those returned through drop boxes or in person.

About 1.2% of the mail-in ballots cast in 2024 were rejected, according to the commission. Of them, 40.7% were rejected because the signature on the return envelope didn't match the one on file or was incomplete, and 10% were rejected because they lacked any signature. Another 17.8% were rejected because they were not received by the state's deadline.

Those deadlines vary from state to state. In California, for instance, mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive as many as seven days afterward and still be counted, according to NCSL. Colorado, by contrast, requires mail-in ballots to be received by 7 p.m. on Election Day. Some states give military and overseas voters additional time for ballots to arrive after Election Day.

In a June ruling, the Supreme Court upheld states' authority to count mail-in ballots received after Election Day, provided they were cast on time and meet state deadlines.

## Mail ballots a week before Election Day

Voters should be aware that, generally, it may take longer than they expect for ballots to reach election offices, and that postmarks may not be applied the day they mail their ballot.

This is because the U.S. Postal Service has been overhauling its operations, which over time has included reduced pickups at many postal locations and increased travel times for mail to reach regional processing centers where postmarks are applied. The upshot is that the agency expects longer delays between when mail is sent and when it is postmarked, according to a Postal Service rule that took effect in December 2025.

In practice, this means some mail doesn't begin moving through the system until at least the day after you mail it, so the postmark isn't applied the day you mailed it. In some cases — i.e., ahead of weekends or holidays — it could take longer for a postmark to be applied, according to the Brookings Institution, a think tank.

# HOW RECENT U.S. POSTAL SERVICE RULE CHANGES PUT MAIL VOTERS AT RISK

## (and What You Can Do to Ensure Your Vote Counts!)

Print This Page as a PDF

### Mail-in voting is critical to many elderly, disabled, and rural voters, hourly-employees and non-drivers, for whom travel to a polling place on Election Day is challenging or impossible.

Read More

## WHAT CHANGED?

The United States Postal Service (USPS) published **a new rule** that took effect on December 24, 2025, stating that mail might not receive a postmark on the same day the Postal Service takes possession of it, i.e., the day you mail it. 

Because election officials in many states qualify mail-in ballots based on the postmark date, this new rule causes problems for thousands of eligible voters who rely on mail-in ballots, putting them at risk for having their votes disqualified should their ballots be postmarked past the deadline—despite having mailed them prior to Election Day. 

Additionally, delayed postmarking could affect voter registration forms and absentee ballot applications, which also rely on postmark dates to determine whether deadlines are met. 

**In all 44 states covered by the National Voter Registration Act** , election officials have to accept voter registration applications postmarked by the deadline, meaning the new rule will affect who gets access to a ballot in the first place.

The USPS claims it isn’t changing its postmark policy, but is instead merely codifying existing practices.
